title: Good ayis are always on assignment — what a domestic-work consultant really sells isn't information
dek: Domestic work is a supply-led industry: good ayis never reach the open market, and the consultant's hard part isn't closing the deal but the after-sales replacement; both employer and ayi are just pass-throughs for a wage.
why: A frontline post-00s domestic-work consultant lays out a neglected essential-need industry: matching mechanics, pricing, off-platform deals, boundaries — high information density, and the second half is worth more.
who: Dual-income families hiring or about to hire a yuesao or yuer sao, and founders and investors watching domestic work and local life services.
skip: From 1:35:37, the twins-family picture-book interview segment is more story than substance — fast-forward it.

points.h: Good ayis are always on assignment
points.body: This market has a circulation paradox: an ayi with good reviews never reaches the open market. She works for one family for two or three years, and the moment she leaves she's referred straight into the next household. The ones actually circulating on the market are usually the ones nobody could be satisfied with, however many families looked them over. So the industry's core contradiction is a supply problem — where good ayis come from and how they get discovered. A domestic-work company is essentially more like a human resources company: it has to recruit, train and re-match.

points.h: Every woman in this trade has a story
points.body: The ayi profile clusters in third- and fourth-tier cities and even poor villages, aged 30 to 45, many divorced or single. Live-in sisters spend little time with their own families and give their time to another household. Two obvious traits mark their choice of this work: they like children, and they want to earn — not to sit comfortably in the village farming and drinking tea, but to pack up everything they own, buy a green-skin train ticket and squeeze their way to Shanghai.

There has to be a sense of boundaries and proportion between ayi and employer — not just for the ayi, but for the employer too. Some people spoil the ayi past all reason, but people always take a mile when given an inch. More delicate still: a live-in ayi is together with the family 24 hours a day, and may know more about the household's private life than blood relatives do — the pressure is heavy. Some mothers are doing widow-style parenting with the father absent, and it's the ayi who ends up keeping the mother company for longer; the two become teammates.

points.h: Employer and ayi are both pass-throughs for a wage
points.body: To the employer she looks like a pass-through for a wage, and the same is true from the ayi's side: the money arrives by WeChat transfer each month, and immediately two children's tuition goes out, then the household living expenses, transferred straight away. For many yuesao and yuer sao, the income is the most important or even the only source for their family, which is why her role as wife within the family structure carries such weight. That also explains why employers care about the ayi's family background — you're not hiring a company employee, and her stability is directly tied to her family situation.

points.h: How ten pages of job requirements don't scare the ayi off
points.body: The longest yuesao job spec I've seen ran a full ten pages, at a price that was only the market average. The employer thinks that writing out every minute and second means the ayi will execute like a robot, but people are emotional. The consultant doesn't forward it directly; she first calls to lay the groundwork by voice: asking about luggage, giving directions, saying the client just wants to know what time you'll arrive, then explaining that company rules require the employer to list requirements and that you can come to me any time with questions. That way the ayi feels she's been handed a guidebook rather than being interrogated.

points.h: Closing the deal isn't hard — replacing someone is the test
points.body: Yuesao work is booked in advance; yuer sao jobs are mostly urgent — an ayi only enters the market once she leaves her previous household, so demand is pressing. Many employers assume that whoever is urgently available must be bad, when in fact it's often the booked one who's the fake. Closing a deal isn't hard for a consultant: as long as the employer has a need and a budget, someone can always be found. The genuinely hard part is the long after-sales tail — the interview can be thrilling, and afterwards there's a certain probability of the thrill dying, and replacing someone is what really tests a consultant's level.

points.h: The hardest deal requires reading the family's core relationship
points.body: The hardest deal: a single mother who is a female executive, wanting a daytime child-development companion, yet hoping this person would also do housework to a cleaner's standard — while the companion's hourly rate is twice a cleaner's. The consultant dealt with an assistant, and the core need was also shaped by the executive mother. The compromise was cleaners for cleaning and companions for companionship, but the mother still had to be won over. The person finally found was the polar opposite of the original spec — the original asked for under 35 with a bilingual kindergarten early-education background; the final hire was a sister approaching 50 with an education background and live-in experience.

points.h: Yuesao start at 15,000; yuer sao depends on age
points.body: In first-tier cities a yuesao's 26-day contract price is generally 15,000 to 16,000 or more; for someone with two or three years' experience who has genuinely cared for a newborn, it's basically 15,000 to 20,000. Shanghai rates for yuer sao: beginners from 7,000, experienced hands depending on age, skills and work history, basically 8,000-plus; stack on English, bilingual, early education or driving and it's 10,000-plus. Prices have risen in recent years partly because more highly educated people are entering the trade, and partly because supply still falls short of demand.

points.h: Consensus and trade norms are what this trade lacks most
points.body: The live-in norm is that the ayi brings her own personal items and the employer provides the big items like bedding, but the two sides of the employment relationship haven't formed a consensus yet. Some think it's lovely when an ayi who's been there a long time grows attached and spends her own wages buying things for the baby; others find it too close. A common situation is a mother who is unhappy that the child is too attached to the ayi. Consultant training teaches this: the person in a household who should be closest to the child is the mother — not the father, and not the grandparents.

points.h: Young people going into domestic work is long past being a meme
points.body: By the time something becomes a meme, the number of people doing it is already beyond what you'd imagine. The contraction of the tutoring industry fed a lot of talent into domestic work; child-development companions are very young, a cohort in their twenties, because jobs are hard to find and this trade provides room and board and responsibility for just one child. After five to eight years of live-in experience, yuying shi and yuesao get older and can't keep up with the child, and shift toward training-instructor roles. But whether you do yuying shi or child-development companion, it's very hard to build a three-to-five-year career plan.

quotes.text: For the employer it's like being a pass-through for a wage, and for a lot of ayis it's really the same.
Because an ayi is a person — a person isn't a machine, a person is in a state where they'll have emotions.

Closing the deal isn't a hard thing for us — we can always help an employer find someone they're satisfied with, as long as they have a need, right, and a budget. But the hard part usually comes later.
I think right now both sides of the employment relationship haven't really formed this consensus, haven't yet accumulated to the point of knowing roughly what state this trade is in.
By the time something has already become a meme, the number of people doing it is already beyond what you'd imagine.
